content.overview: Lighting quality includes distribution as well as average intensity. A specialist uses spatial maps, range and pattern to identify hot spots, edge losses and canopy zones that may require fixture-layout or canopy-management review.

vocabulary.definition: The consistency of measured light distribution across a defined canopy area.
A localized region with substantially higher measured intensity than surrounding canopy positions.
Reduced measured light near the perimeter of the managed canopy relative to interior positions.

sections.title: Average can hide extremes
sections.body: Averages should be reviewed with minimum, maximum and spatial pattern. A room may meet an average target while containing biologically different bright and dim zones.

sections.title: Fixture geometry shapes the map
sections.body: Fixture spacing, mounting height, overlap, room boundaries and canopy height influence distribution. Re-map after meaningful layout or canopy changes.

sections.title: Uniformity decisions need crop context
sections.body: A spatial pattern matters most when it is repeatable and aligns with crop architecture or response. Do not redesign a room from one noisy map.

workedExamples: If average PPFD stays similar after raising fixtures but range narrows and corners improve, uniformity may have improved even though the mean changed little.
commonMistakes: Changing several fixture variables before repeating the same grid.
content.practicalApplication: Compare two mapped light distributions using average, range and spatial pattern, then recommend the next measurement or authorized adjustment.
content.summary: Uniformity is a spatial property; it cannot be inferred from one number.
